content:
"How do people learn to use Claude Code like Boris?"

Claude Code creator Boris Cherny (@bcherny ) was asked by Diana Hu ( @sdianahu ) at Startup School 2026.

Boris Cherny: "Maybe don’t listen to the LinkedIn influencers.

The thing about the model is that everyone is looking for one weird trick to make it work, but that simply doesn’t exist. There is nothing like that.

You have to approach the model empirically. Give it a task that is too hard. Give it the tools to verify its work, just as you would use those tools yourself if you were doing the task. 
See where it struggles, and then fix the problem with better prompting, a skill, or if the model is missing context, an MCP connection that allows it to retrieve the context it needs.

That is basically it.

It sounds very simple. I think people tend to overthink and overengineer it because, in many ways, that is how we had to build systems in the past."

content:
Another WTF moment.

A developer just open-sourced a coding agent harness that boots 245x faster than Claude Code. It's called jcode. You launch it and the first frame renders in 14 milliseconds. Claude Code takes 3,436. One active session uses 27.8 MB of RAM. Claude Code uses 386.6. Run ten sessions in parallel and jcode holds at 117 MB while OpenCode swells to 3.2 GB.

Each agent has a semantic memory graph instead of a scratchpad. Every turn gets embedded as a vector. The graph is queried on every turn for related memories, and a sideagent verifies the hits before injecting them into context. Consolidation runs in the background to check for stale or conflicting facts. No manual /remember calls. No token burn on lookup tools.

The provider list is 30+ deep. Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Azure, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Groq, Mistral, Perplexity, Fireworks, Ollama, LM Studio, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint you point it at. Ran out of tokens on your first ChatGPT Pro sub? /account swaps to the second.

Then there's Swarm. Spawn two agents in the same repo and the server manages them. When agent A edits a file agent B has been reading, agent B gets pinged and can check the diff. Agents can DM each other, broadcast to the room, or spawn their own worker teams for parallel tasks. Groups, channels, and completion statuses are handled automatically.

The UI has live side panels that render mermaid diagrams inline. To make it fast, the author wrote a Rust mermaid renderer 1800x faster than the JavaScript one, then wrote a custom terminal called Handterm because no existing terminal could do smooth partial-line scrolling.

Self-dev mode is where it gets wild. Tell your agent to enter self-dev and it starts editing jcode's own source code, rebuilds the binary, reloads it live, and keeps working across your existing sessions. You can also resume broken sessions from Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or pi directly inside jcode. Anthropic's cache goes cold at the 5-minute mark and you're staring down a big cache miss on your next turn? The UI warns you before you spend the tokens.

Written in Rust. MIT licensed. Runs on macOS, Windows, Linux, and Termux. Sitting at 11.2k stars with a native iOS app coming.

content:
First  what Claude Code actually is. And why it's fundamentally different from ChatGPT or Copilot.

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It works in the terminal, the desktop app, and your IDE. It can read files, run commands, edit code, and call external tools. Under the hood, it runs an agentic loop.

The distinction is structural. GitHub Copilot suggests the next line of code based on what you've already written. ChatGPT answers questions about code you paste into it. Neither one understands your project as a whole.

Claude Code operates as a full coding agent. It reads your entire project, understands the structure, and executes development tasks through natural language instructions.

You don't paste code into Claude Code. You point it at your codebase and talk to it in English: "Add error handling to the API routes in src/api/. Follow the pattern from auth.ts."

It reads auth.ts. It reads every API route. It adds error handling that matches your existing pattern. Across 8 files. In 30 seconds.

The shift: from "AI that answers questions about code" to "AI that writes, edits, tests, and deploys code inside your project." That's the gap between a chatbot and an agent.

my highest-probability guess: SSI has found a brain-inspired way to make an AI continually learn.

today’s frontier models learn mostly during training. afterward, their core knowledge is largely frozen. they consume enormous datasets and still fail strangely when a problem falls outside their training.

SSI may have an early system that can:

• learn a new skill from very few experiences
• recognize when an approach is failing before reaching the final answer
• update itself without erasing old skills
• transfer one lesson into completely different problems
• keep learning after deployment

think of it like a gifted teenager instead of a finished encyclopedia. it may not begin knowing every profession, but it could rapidly learn any profession.

the evidence lines up almost too cleanly:

ilya called poor generalization the fundamental limitation of current AI. models “generalize dramatically worse than people.”
he described SSI’s target as a “superintelligent 15-year-old” capable of learning any job.
when asked how to create human-like learning, he said there is a machine-learning principle he has opinions about but cannot discuss publicly.
WSJ now reports that SSI’s secret research focuses on “overlooked aspects of how the human brain functions.”
Nvidia received rare access to the research, made a substantial investment, gave SSI 10x more compute, and agreed to let SSI help shape future computing platforms.

my technical guess:

experience → internal judgment → self-correction → durable learning → transfer → repeat

the internal judgment may be the brain-inspired component.

humans do not wait until the end of a 10,000-step task to know they are failing. emotions, intuition and judgment provide constant feedback. ilya has argued that AI needs an equivalent internal “value function.”

this could also explain SSI’s central promise: capability and safety trained together.

the same mechanism that teaches the AI what works may also teach it what it should care about.

my confidence is roughly 70% on human-like generalization plus continual learning, and 40% that an internal value system is the central mechanism.

the simplest description:

an AI whose intelligence compounds from experience, with its values learning inside the same loop.

“We have driven more than 380,000 miles of unsupervised Robotaxi across six cities in two states. Zero notable incidents.
content:
During the Q2 earnings call, Ashok once again made the case for vision-only:

“We have driven more than 380,000 miles of unsupervised Robotaxi across six cities in two states. Zero notable incidents. Historically, the so-called experts claimed you need LiDARs, radars, HD maps — the entire kitchen sink — to drive safely. Here we show that is not true. You can have safe, comfortable, and affordable autonomy with just cameras.”

I am one of those so-called experts. I spent over a decade working on sensor fusion. Real data shows that fusing computer vision with an active sensor like radar improves both true positives (actually detecting real objects) and false positives (avoiding phantom objects that aren’t there) by roughly an order of magnitude versus vision alone.

But here’s the uncomfortable truth: Ashok is right. In every single failure case I ever studied, the information was already present in the image. It was never an input problem. It was a processing problem: the AI fails to recognize what is clearly visible in the image to any human looking at it.

Fusion is a quick win that papers over weak vision. You hit a ceiling fast. Tesla started from first principles and understood something most of the industry still refuses to accept: all the information you need is already in the image. No other sensor can give you more.

During Rivian’s next-gen autonomy presentation, RJ himself highlighted a pedestrian that was perfectly visible in the camera but lost by their perception stack — only to be “saved” by radar fusion. That is not a success story for fusion. It is an admission that the vision system failed on information that was right there.

The experts who insist fusion is required for safety are mostly hiding the real difficulty: it takes an enormous amount of data, training infrastructure, and specialized methods to train for fixed-point inference to make pure vision work at the required reliability. That is the hard path. It is also the only path that actually scales.

More thoughts in my article from January.

content:
Weighing the evidence I've seen, I don't believe ARC-AGI-3 was directly targeted by Opus 5 eg synthetic RL envs or anything like that.

Instead what I think is happening is the Claude Code/Work harness is getting trained into the model.

You see this in the significantly sharper strategy and context carry-forward through conversation turns coming from the raw model, sans harness.

So, the Opus 5 raw API got a big boost, bringing it closer to capability previously dependent on the harness.

But for CC/Work users, you wouldn't see as much improvement (that the big v3 score jump might suggest) because the harness was already doing most of it.

At launch I predicted the majority of progress on ARC v3 this year would come from harness improvement.

And that the most general advancements to on-the-fly world modeling would eventually get trained into the models like we saw with AI reasoning.

We've certainly seen great harness ideas proliferating already (see the Duke paper published today).

But the speed at which this behavior got trained into the models surprised me.

If I'm right, we should expect each LLM family to "unlock" the v3 format with a relatively large jump as they acquire the ability to do basic on-the-fly world modeling without a harness.

And then it will be a grind up on score from there as model intelligence increases to deal with harder goals to acquire, higher abstraction compositional generalization, and longer planning horizons.

title:
Eric Schmidt was asked a technical question about open source and answered with the map of the next fifty years.

The winner won’t be the smartest model. It’ll be the one four billion people never had
content:
Eric Schmidt was asked a technical question about open source and answered with the map of the next fifty years.

The winner won’t be the smartest model. It’ll be the one four billion people never had to choose.

Schmidt: “China is competing with open weights and open training data, and the US is largely and majority focused on closed weights, closed data.”

That isn’t a product decision. It’s a distribution decision. And distribution has beaten quality in every contest that ever mattered.

Schmidt: “The majority of the world, think of it as the Belt and Road initiative, are going to use Chinese models and not American models.”

The first Belt and Road was ports, rail, and highways. This one doesn’t get poured. It gets downloaded.

Every piece of infrastructure ever built was indifferent to what moved across it. A road doesn’t tell you where to go.

A model does.

Schmidt: “The American models are typically using 16-bit precision for their training. The Chinese are pushing 8 and now even 4.”

Every bit they drop is a cheaper device that can run it.

We cut off their chips to slow them down. Scarcity made their models small. Small is what crosses a border.

We designed their advantage.

Not better. Present.

America is building the best model on earth and metering it. China is building one that’s good enough and giving it away.

A model isn’t software. It’s a compressed set of judgments about what’s true, what’s askable, and what a reasonable answer sounds like.

Install that as a country’s default and you haven’t sold them a tool. You’ve set the limits of what occurs to them.

That isn’t censorship. Censorship leaves a mark.

A question that never occurs to you doesn’t feel like a restriction. It feels like the edge of the world.

Every empire before this one had to teach the world its language first. Missionaries, schoolteachers, garrisons, printing presses.

Every one of them ran through a human being who could hesitate, doubt, or be talked out of it.

AI arrives already speaking yours.

It doesn’t ask you to change. It changes you in your own voice.

The first ideology in history that doesn’t need believers. It only needs to be installed.

Schmidt: “I’d much rather have the proliferation of large language models and that learning be done based on Western values.”

He’s right, and we’re playing it backwards. We treat openness like a giveaway, as if the weights were the crown jewels.

Openness is the one advantage an authoritarian can’t copy.

An open model can be read, probed, and torn apart by anyone who doubts it. A system that has to control the answer can never afford to publish the reasoning.

China opens its weights to spread them. America could open its weights to be trusted. Only one of those compounds.

A closed American model wins the benchmark. An open American model wins the default. Centuries get built out of defaults.

Schmidt: “We also have to watch to make sure that the proliferation of these models for handheld devices is under American control.”

That’s the ground. Not data centers. Not cloud contracts. Pockets.

The frontier race has five contenders and the whole world watching. This one has no audience at all. It plays out on hardware too cheap to run an American model, and goes to whoever bothered to show up.

We keep asking who reaches AGI first. The question that settles the century is smaller and much harder to take back.

Four billion people are going to ask a machine what happened in their own country. Whose answer do they get?

Nobody votes on that. It’s decided by whatever was already installed.

America has the best AI ever built.

The only way to lose this era is to keep it.

content:
Every book burning in history was performed in public. The Inquisition wanted witnesses. The Nazis wanted photographs. The one happening right now shreds up to a million books per order and comes with a nondisclosure agreement, because the people running it understand exactly how it looks.

ISBNdb, a database company that spent years helping libraries and booksellers find books, now brokers anonymous bulk purchases for AI labs. Its own website admits that "AI company destroys two million books" is a headline nobody wants, then offers a strict NDA on every engagement and coaches buyers to describe the shredding as digital preservation. A rare book dealer in Haarlem received an order for nearly 3,000 titles. Sellers across Germany, Switzerland, and Spain report the same overnight bulk buys. Books with almost no surviving copies are going into the spine-cutters.

And the law is holding the door open. Judge Alsup ruled in Bartz v. Anthropic that buying a book, slicing off its spine, and destroying it after scanning is transformative fair use. The pirated half of the same case cost $1.5 billion in settlement, roughly $3,000 per book. So the market learned the lesson instantly. Piracy costs $3,000 a copy. Destruction costs nothing.

Google scanned 25 million library books, returned every single one, and spent 11 years in court defending it. The shredder approach cleared court in ten months. Guess which method the industry chose.

When your business model needs an NDA to survive contact with the public, you already know what the business is. The book burners of history at least stood next to the fire.

title: In the last few weeks, frontier AI models have reportedly solved long-standing mathematical problems. This suggests that current AI tools might largely automate parts of what mathematicians used to do
content:
In the last few weeks, frontier AI models have reportedly solved long-standing mathematical problems. This suggests that current AI tools might largely automate parts of what mathematicians used to do in the near future. To put some context to it, the 'near future' means that next five years.

Well. Yeah. If you have been following how recent AI systems have been evolving, you should not be too surprised.

The famous mathematician Gowers (@wtgowers) attended a workshop on AI and mathematics where participants produced something called the Leiden Declaration. It appears to position professional mathematics with respect to AI.

I would say they are circling the wagons, that is, they are on the defensive. Here are some statements from the declaration cited by Gowers:

“Credit and responsibility continue to belong to humans within the mathematical community and should not be given to automated systems. (…) material should not be used as training data without consent, and publishing agreements should allow authors to opt out of the use of their work in this way (…) Demand that mathematical results continue to be published in peer-reviewed venues such as journals, proceedings, and books.”

To sum it up, the mathematicians are saying that we have this nice system we have constructed since the 1970s, and we want to keep it.

They seem unaware that most of mathematics was built before the current peer-review system arrived on the scene in the second half of the twentieth century.

So what does Gowers says? From my reading, he expects that incentive structures for professional mathematicians will be seriously disrupted. Circling the wagons will not work. He concludes that the successful mathematician of the future might be more of an educator than someone who proves theorems…

“Maybe that is what the ‘research mathematicians’ of the future should do: make a selection from a vast sea of AI-generated mathematics and write a book about it in such a way that other mathematicians can read the book and feel the kind of enrichment that we feel when we get to grips with an area of mathematics.”

Maybe. Maybe.

But another possibility is that if you are seeking to understand a specific concept, you will ask the AI to give you an explanation taylored just for you. And maybe pedagogical content will be, by default, generated by AI (or, at least, assisted by AI).

So what is happening to mathematics? It feels like a true technological singularity: progress is too fast for anyone to understand.

Once the weights are public, anyone on Earth can run, host, audit, or improve them independently. No Chinese company has to be in the loop, not for training data access after release, not for inference, not for updates.

That’s the whole point of open weights: true decentralization. Host it yourself, run it on US/EU servers, or use any non-Chinese provider. The model itself becomes a public good, not a corporate or national asset.

Transparency + free replication = the opposite of control.

content:
最近のオープンモデルを政府が禁止するだの擁護の公開書簡だののゴタゴタで一人だけ署名しなかったAnthropicは今回のヴィランのクズとしてバチボコにされている。それに対してダリオがレスバ記事をアップした。「Anthropicはオープンモデルを禁止しろなんて一度も言ってない」との事。えっ！？そうだっけ？ダリオが懸念してる事①中国政府のような権威主義的な国家が米国より強いAIを作ってしまってそれで軍事的に優位になったり国民の弾圧に使ってしまう危険。つまり中国が強いAIを持つのは危険と言ってるのであってオープンモデルかどうかは関係ない②アラインメントされてないAIがサイバー攻撃や生物兵器に悪用されるリスクが危険。そしてオープンモデルにはガードレールなんて無いんだからクローズモデルよりリスクが高いのは事実。とは言え米国政府がオープンモデル禁止しても意味無いっす。だって米国にサイバー攻撃するのは外国なんだから。
だから本当にやらなきゃいけないのはオープンモデル禁止じゃなくて以下の３つ。①中国にAIチップを売らないようにする②大規模蒸留を取り締まる③モデルは安全性テストを通してからリリースする。オープンとかクローズとか関係なくやる。
オープンモデル擁護の公開書簡についても、ダリオは大体同意しているとの事。ただし、「オープンモデルの方が安全策を容易に開発できる」とか「オープンモデルの方がサイバー防御側に有利」とか書いてる点には同意できないので署名せんだけの事。むしろ逆じゃね？オープンな高性能モデルを使ってウイルスを作ってパンデミック起こされたらどうする？防御側にも同様にオープンな高性能モデルがあったとて、イチからワクチンとか作ってたら数年必要だよ。だったらモデルをクローズにして最初からウイルス作るような悪用させない方がマシだよなあ？
…との事。ダリオは「オープンモデルを禁止しろなんて言ってない」とか言うけど、たしかに文字通りには言ってない。しかし「オープンモデルが引き起こすリスクが許せない」と言ってるんだからオープンモデルの規制を求めてるも同然。屁理屈を言うなよ

過去に保存された分は消えないので、「保存した履歴の表示と削除」から自分で消す必要があります。

期限のある設定ではありません。

現在、モデルの頭脳にあたる調整パラメーターを一般公開する「オープンウェイト（Open Weights）」と、技術を非公開にする「独占モデル」の境界線を巡って、激しい主導権争いが起きています。

事の発端は、NVIDIAのジェン・スン・ファンCEOらが署名した「オープンウェイトと米国のAIリーダーシップ」という書簡です。OpenAIのサム・アルトマンCEOもこの動きを支持していますが、ここには高度な政治的・ビジネス的戦略が隠されています。米国側は自国の「適度にコントロールされた」オープンモデルを推奨する一方で、急速に進化する中国製の巨大なオープンウェイトモデル（Qwenなど）を制限・排除したいという思惑が見え隠れしているのです。

さらに、ビジネスモデルにおける矛盾も浮き彫りになっています。OpenAIは「オープン」を掲げつつも、最先端のフラグシップモデルは非公開のままにしています。これは自社が「ゲートキーパー（門番）」として市場を支配し続けるため、そして将来的なIPOを有利に進めるための防衛策と言えますね。もし特定のタスクに特化し、家庭用デバイスでもサクサク動く「特化型LLM」が普及すれば、巨大AI企業の独占市場が脅かされることになるからです。

AI競争は、すでに「どこかがゴールして終わり」という単純なレースではありません。どれだけ莫大な資金とエネルギーを消費し続けられるかという「資本燃費率」の消耗戦に突入しています。

これからの技術選定やビジネス戦略においては、単なるツール選びを超えて、こうした輸出規制や地政学的リスク、そして資本効率の裏側まで見極める視点が非常に重要になります！

content:
【AIがBlenderを直接操作するMCPの衝撃！3Dプリンティングに潜む「製造の壁」とは？】
👉  https://t.co/ulkOZxPMbz
Model Context Protocol (MCP) を使って、LLMからBlenderのPython API（bpy）を直接制御し、自然言語から3Dモデルを自動作成する驚きのワークフローが登場しました！🤖✨

画面上で指示するだけで、Blender上でコードが動いてあっという間に3Dのベースモデルが構築されちゃいます。これはプロトタイピングがめちゃくちゃ捗りますね！

でも、ここに実務ならではの落とし穴があります…！🕳️
画面上でどんなに綺麗にレンダリングされていても、実際に3Dプリンターで印刷（スライス）しようとするとエラーになってしまうことがあるんです。
なぜなら、AIは画面上の見た目を作れても、「物理的な製造ルール」を完全には理解していないからですね。

具体的には以下のような「製造の壁」があります：
・隙間のない「水密（Watertight）な構造」になっていないと、スライサーソフト（印刷用コードを作るソフト）が正常に処理できません。
・構造の厚みが足りないと、印刷中に強度が持たず土台から剥がれ落ちて壊れてしまいます。

つまり、AIが生成したモデルをそのまま使うのではなく、印刷前の数分〜15分程度の「クリーンアップ（手動による形状の修正）」が実は一番重要な作業になります。AIを「完成品メーカー」ではなく「高速な下地作成ツール」として位置づけるのが、現場で上手く使いこなすコツですね！👨‍💻🛠️

なお、AI生成コードは制限のない環境で実行されるため、大切なデータを守るためにも「使い捨てのプロジェクト」で安全にテストするのがおすすめです！

「顔の表情（一貫性）」を美しく保つ能力がズバ抜けています！
動画の途中で顔が別人になってしまうのを防ぎたいなら、間違いなくこの選択肢が最有力です。Wan 2.2とScail-2をハイブリッドで使うワークフローもコミュニティで熱心に開発されています。

content:
【ComfyUI】VRAM不足エラー（OOM）を撃退！最新アップデート後のメモリ枯渇問題を解決する4つのアプローチ💡

画像生成を楽しんでいるときに突然発生する「VRAM不足（Out of Memory）」エラー、本当に困ってしまいますよね……。😢
実はこれ、GPUのスペック不足だけが原因ではなく、最新アップデートに含まれるメモリ管理の不具合や、外部ツールの干渉が引き金になっていることが多いんです！

そこで、快適な創作環境を取り戻すためのトラブルシューティングをまとめてみました！✨

1️⃣ 起動引数のクリーンアップ
メモリを節約するためのオプション引数（`--smart-memory` や `--high-vram` など）を一度すべて外し、デフォルトの状態で起動してみてください。これだけで不具合が解消されるケースがあるんです！

2️⃣ 外部アプリのVRAM占有をチェック
ブラウザの「ハードウェアアクセラレーション」機能が、バックグラウンドでVRAMをこっそり消費していることも。コマンドプロンプトで `nvidia-smi` を実行して、他のプロセスがメモリを奪っていないか確認しましょう。

3️⃣ Gitで安定バージョンにロールバック
直近のアップデートが原因と思われる場合は、一度安定して動いていた過去のバージョンに戻すのが確実です。ターミナルで `git log` を確認し、正常だった時点のコミットへ `git checkout <ハッシュ値>` で戻してみるのがおすすめです。

4️⃣ PyTorchのメモリ断片化対策
環境変数に `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` を設定してみましょう！細切れになって使えなくなったGPUメモリ領域を効率よく結合して、エラーを防いでくれます。

高価なグラフィックボードに買い替える前に、まずはこれらのソフトウェア設定を見直して、スムーズな画像生成ライフを取り戻しましょう！🚀

What if your future wasn't decided by a judge, your boss, or even your own choices...

...but by an AI score you never agreed to?

Edward Snowden has been warning about this for years.

His concern isn't just surveillance—it's what happens when governments use AI to turn surveillance into control.

In parts of China, AI-powered "City Brain" systems can monitor:

• Where you live
• Who you spend time with
• Every public movement
• How you dispose of rubbish
• Whether you follow rules

The more data collected, the more decisions can be automated.

Snowden's warning is simple:

If an algorithm determines you're no longer compliant, it could affect your ability to travel, find work, or participate in everyday life.

His broader concern is that systems built for convenience can gradually become systems of control.

And he argues that these technologies aren't staying inside China.

As governments around the world explore digital IDs, AI-assisted policing, and automated risk scoring, the same underlying ideas are beginning to appear elsewhere.

China may have built the prototype.

The question is whether the rest of the world chooses to follow it.

Technology itself isn't the problem.

The real question is: who controls it—and who does it control?

content: Recent reports have raised alarm about the use of PatronScan, an ID-checking and face-scanning system, at multiple LGBTQ+ bars in San Francisco’s Castro neighborhood. Much of the attention has focused on reports that the system photographs patrons as they enter venues and questions about whether those images are used for facial recognition. A broader privacy concern also deserves scrutiny. For years, PatronScan has marketed itself not just as an ID-verification tool, but as a system that allows bars and clubs to identify patrons, keep records about them, and share information across venues. As one news article published in 2019 documented , PatronScan built a network that allowed participating bars to flag patrons and share information about them with other establishments. And in California, it’s not at all clear how PatronScan’s business model of scanning IDs and sharing the information from those scans with other bars comports with the law. California’s ID privacy law , which was amended in 2018 to add ID “scans,” states that no businesses shall “retain or use” any information from a scanned ID card except for limited purposes such as to verify age, comply with a legal requirement, or prevent fraud. title: Farmers Are Getting Control Of Their Equipment Back
content: For years, John Deere had actively made repairing their tractors near-impossible for anyone but itself and the few "authorized" repair shops—regardless of the ability of its customers to actually visit such shops. Now, in a major win for farmers and right to repair advocates, John Deere must soon provide farmers with not just the tools and resources to finally repair their own John Deere equipment, but also access to future updates for said equipment. In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) brought a suit against farm equipment manufacturer John Deere, alleging John Deere used their control over equipment repair tools and resources to limit the ability of farmers and independent repair providers (IRPs) to repair John Deere equipment. Earlier this month, John Deere reached a settlement with the FTC in which they will immediately make available a tranche of repair resources, then continue to make further resources available until the end of the year. Five states joined the FTC in this suit, and over the next 10 years these states will work alongside the FTC to ensure John Deere complies with this settlement. It is worth noting there is a second, farmer-initiated antitrust lawsuit against John Deere, also concerning a farmer’s right to repair their own equipment. In April, John Deere agreed to a $99 million settlement in that case, which also includes right to repair provisions.
